title: Building fat, two carbons at a time

scenes.visual: three stage panels: transport, activation, elongation
scenes.narration: Everything we do today fits into three stages. Stage one. Transport. ATP-citrate lyase cleaves citrate to deliver acetyl CoA into the cytoplasm. Stage two. Activation. The committed step. Acetyl CoA carboxylase spends an ATP to make malonyl CoA, locking the cell into building fat. Stage three. Elongation. Fatty acid synthase runs a four-step cycle over and over, adding two carbons each pass until it reaches palmitate. Notice the logic: get the bricks to the site, commit irreversibly, then build. If you remember nothing else, remember transport, activation, elongation, in that order.
scenes.slideTitle: The Three Stages of Fatty Acid Synthesis
scenes.notes: Everything we do today fits into three stages. Stage one, transport: ATP-citrate lyase cleaves citrate to deliver acetyl CoA into the cytoplasm. Stage two, activation, the committed step: acetyl CoA carboxylase spends an ATP to make malonyl CoA, locking the cell into building fat. Stage three, elongation: fatty acid synthase runs a four-step cycle over and over, adding two carbons each pass until it reaches palmitate. Notice the logic, get the bricks to the site, commit irreversibly, then build. If you remember nothing else, remember transport, activation, elongation, in that order.

scenes.visual: ACC + biotin swinging arm; one-way commit gate
scenes.narration: Here is the decision point of the entire pathway. Acetyl CoA carboxylase takes acetyl CoA, bicarbonate, and ATP and produces malonyl CoA. This is the committed step, the reaction that says the cell is now making fat and nothing else. The enzyme depends on biotin, a vitamin cofactor whose job is to carry carbon dioxide. Think of biotin as a swinging arm that grabs a carboxyl group and delivers it. Because this step is committed and irreversible, it is exactly where regulation should sit. And indeed, this enzyme is the master control valve we will return to.

scenes.visual: CRDR cycle x7, chain counter 2 to 16
scenes.narration: Now we build. Fatty acid synthase is one enzyme complex that runs a repeating four-step cycle, condensation, reduction, dehydration, reduction. Remember it as CRDR. Each turn of the cycle joins the growing chain to a fresh two-carbon unit and then chemically grooms the new linkage into a saturated stretch. The cycle is not run once, but seven times, because each pass adds two carbons and we are aiming for a 16-carbon product, palmitate. The elegance is that a single enzyme assembly does the same four moves repeatedly, like a machine stamping out identical parts on an assembly line.

scenes.visual: primer + extender, CO2 leaves, energy drop
scenes.narration: Here is the chemical trick that makes synthesis go. We have a primer, the acetyl group, and an extender, the malonyl group. When they condense, the malonyl loses its extra carboxyl as carbon dioxide. That decarboxylation is the engine. Releasing carbon dioxide is so thermodynamically favorable that it drags the otherwise sluggish condensation forward, the way letting go of a heavy weight pulls the whole rope along. The product, acetoacetyl-ACP, forms readily because the cell paid for that carbon dioxide earlier with ATP. So the carbon we added in stage two leaves here, but its purpose was always to power this step.

scenes.visual: energy hill vs pay ATP first
scenes.narration: Step back and ask a fair question. Why spend an ATP to attach a carbon dioxide in stage two only to throw that same carbon dioxide away during condensation? It looks wasteful. The answer is that the cell is buying thermodynamics. Direct condensation of two acetyl units is unfavorable and would barely proceed. By investing one ATP to carboxylate first, the cell stores energy in malonyl CoA. Then, when that carbon dioxide is released, its departure makes condensation strongly downhill. It is a gambit. Pay up front, release on demand, and gain control over a reaction that otherwise would not run. Every carbon still traces back to acetyl CoA.
